issues.legal_issue: Civil courts are barred from reconsidering the merits or propriety of final orders made under a special statutory scheme, but may examine a challenge that would establish the order is a nullity.
material_facts: The landlords obtained permission to sue for ejectment after the District Magistrate refused permission and the Commissioner granted it on revision.
The tenants challenged the validity of the Commissioner's permission in the civil suit, and the High Court held that the permission was invalid.
The statutory scheme made the Commissioner's order final subject to State Government revision and provided a statutory review process.

The Supreme Court held that ordinary challenges to correctness or propriety were barred, while a challenge alleging a fundamental defect that would make an order a nullity could be examined by a civil court.
issues.conclusion: The civil court's jurisdiction was excluded for challenges to the correctness or propriety of the statutory orders, but not for a challenge that, if upheld, would establish that an order was a nullity. The tenants' challenge to the scope of the Commissioner's revisional power did not make the permission a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(4) and 16 of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, exclude civil-court review of the merits or propriety of covered orders; the statutory review process, including revision under section 7-F, supports that exclusion. The exclusion does not prevent a civil court from examining a fundamental defect that would render an order a nullity, such as want of authority or breach of a mandatory procedural requirement. This approach is supported by Secretary of State for India in Council v. Roy Jatindra Nath Chowdhury, Secretary of State v. Mask & Co., and M/s Kamala Mills Ltd. v. State of Bombay. Lala Shri Bhagwan v. Shri Ram Chand recognizes the quasi-judicial character of the proceedings and the relevance of natural justice, but did not decide the civil-court-bar question.

rule.if: civil_case_challenges_special_authority_order and special_law_makes_order_final and alternative_review_remedy_exists and (challenge_attacks_merits_or_propriety or challenge_alleges_fundamental_nullity)

predicates.civil_case_challenges_special_authority_: A party asks a civil court to examine an order made by an authority acting under a special statutory scheme.
predicates.special_law_makes_order_final: The special law makes the authority's order final, expressly or by necessary implication.
predicates.alternative_review_remedy_exists: The special law provides a review or revision process for a party aggrieved by the order.
predicates.challenge_attacks_merits_or_propriety: The party disputes the order's correctness or propriety without alleging a defect that would make it a nullity.
predicates.challenge_alleges_fundamental_nullity: The party alleges a fundamental defect that, if established, would make the order legally void.

issues.definition: When a civil case challenges a final order made under a special scheme with an alternative review process, the civil court may examine the challenge only if it alleges a fundamental defect that would make the order a nullity.

issues.legal_issue: A revisional authority may correct an erroneous refusal to grant permission even when the governing provision does not limit revision to jurisdictional errors.
material_facts: The District Magistrate refused the landlords permission to sue for ejectment.
On the landlords' revision, the Commissioner considered the refusal erroneous and granted permission.
The High Court treated the Commissioner's power as equivalent to the jurisdictional limits on revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and held the permission invalid.

The Supreme Court held that the governing provision authorized revision where the District Magistrate had acted illegally, with material irregularity, or had wrongly refused to act, and that the last ground allowed correction of an erroneous refusal.
issues.conclusion: The Commissioner's revisional power was not confined to jurisdictional errors, and the Commissioner could correct the District Magistrate's erroneous refusal to grant permission. The permission was not invalid on the ground adopted by the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(3) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, the Commissioner could interfere if the District Magistrate acted illegally, acted with material irregularity, or wrongly refused to act. The phrase “wrongly refused to act” encompassed an erroneous refusal to grant permission; the provision did not import the jurisdictional limits of section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The later amendment to section 3(3), which expressly referred to correctness, legality, and propriety, and the State Government's broad power under section 7-F supported the conclusion that the revisional power was wide.

predicates.revision_proceeding_reviews_permission_o: A party seeks revision of an authority's decision on whether permission to bring a proceeding should be granted.
predicates.original_authority_refused_permission: The authority that first considered the request refused permission.
predicates.revisional_authority_considers_refusal_e: The revisional authority considers that the refusal was an error.

issues.definition: When a revision concerns a permission decision, the original authority refused permission, and the revisional authority considers the refusal erroneous, the revisional authority may correct the refusal.
